This week, we reaffirmed that criminal justice and the rule of law are at the heart of building safer societies and protecting people and the planet. For decades, This Congress has helped move the criminal justice agenda forward, strengthening our shared understanding of crime, advancing criminal justice, and steadily building the international framework we need to meet common challenges. Five years ago, when we gathered in Kyoto under the extraordinary circumstances of a global pandemic, Member States adopted the Kyoto Declaration. That declaration became a bridge between where we were and where we needed to go, laying the groundwork for new normative and international instruments, including the Kyoto Model Strategies on reducing reoffending. This week here in Abu Dhabi, we have kept the legacy alive and have extended that bridge even further. On our very first day, you, the Member States, adopted the Abu Dhabi Declaration by acclamation, setting out a global blueprint for confronting crime as it evolves in today's digital age. By that confirmation, Abu Dhabi demonstrated that consensus is still possible, even at a time when multilateralism is considered under considerable pressure. Even when countries come to the table with different perspectives, different priorities, and different interests, we can find common ground when we focus on collective challenges that we face. This is especially so when we are guided by our true North Star, namely the needs of the people we are here to protect. The trends and the dynamics of crime are changing rapidly. The nature and scale of crime worldwide and its impact on our common aspiration for security, development and the rule of law are evolving towards an existential threat to humanity and the planet. This reality calls for more, not less, cooperation. For more, not less, interoperability. This, ladies and gentlemen, is an important message to take home from Abu Dhabi. Over the course of the last week, Member States have put commitments behind the words of the Declaration. I am therefore pleased to announce that member states made 61 pledges this week. I am also aware of many more commitments made at various levels between agencies, institutions, countries, and between regions. These publicly announced pledges represent 61 steps forward, 61 commitments to carry with us, 61 checkpoints on the road ahead. Together, they give us a clear direction for the next chapter of our journey. Minister. With this, and we have seen what we have done, I really want to underscore and invite the UAE to continue championing the initiative and helping us in carrying this momentum forward. Of course, the responsibility for delivering pledges rests with each and every member state that made them. Our collective responsibility is to keep them in view to return to these commitments, to track the progress, and to maintain momentum through the Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice as the intergovernmental follow-up body of this Congress. Throughout the week, delegation after delegation has emphasized the urgency of action and the need for scaling impact. The support pledged by the UAE will help us keep that course and advance implementation of the Abu Dhabi Declaration towards 2031. On our part, UNODC, as the custodian of this journey, will be there alongside the Member States, helping to carry these commitments from this room into real change in people's lives. So, this is not the end of the road. In many ways, it is not even the end of this Congress. It is the beginning of the Abu Dhabi cycle. Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, Madam Executive Director, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, I have the honor to speak on behalf of the European Union and its member states. As this Congress draws to a close, we warmly thank the United Arab Emirates for your generous hospitality and leadership, the President and Chairs for guiding us so well through our deliberations, and Executive Director Monica Juma, our Executive Director, and the Secretariat for your dedication and excellent support. The report of the Congress brings together the Abu Dhabi Declaration, the deliberations in the plenary, and the salient points and conclusions emerging from the workshops. These priorities should guide our follow-up in Vienna and our cooperation on the ground. We encourage the Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice to draw on the Congress report in carrying forward the declaration and the conclusions emerging from our discussions, through focused exchanges on implementation, practical challenges and results. We also thank the practitioners, civil society representatives, researchers, and young people whose contributions have enriched these discussions and helped connect our policy commitments with experience on the ground. Our responsibility is now to ensure that the work recorded in the Congress report leads to sustained cooperation and tangible improvements in people's lives. Mr. President, the discussions in plenary and the workshops have brought together questions that must be addressed together in practice. How to prevent crime, how to ensure equal access to justice, how to anticipate emerging threats, and how to strengthen cooperation in the digital age. On prevention, we must invest in the conditions that enable people and communities to resist violence and exploitation. Education, social inclusion, support for families and opportunities for young people belong at the heart of this effort. Women, children and young people must have a meaningful role in shaping the policies intended to protect them. Preventing the recruitment of children by criminal networks requires both early support and effective action against those who exploit them. On access to justice, our institutions must be independent, impartial, accessible and accountable. Legal aid, fair trial guarantees and effective remedies must be available throughout the criminal justice process. Victims need protection, information and support adapted to their circumstances. Child-friendly, Gender-transformative and trauma-informed approaches, alongside appropriate restorative justice opportunities, can help justice systems respond more effectively to the people they serve. On effective international cooperation, we should strengthen our capacity to understand emerging criminal markets, identify vulnerabilities, and assess whether our responses work. Better data collection and analysis should inform prevention, operational cooperation, and the allocation of resources. We encourage closer collaboration among public authorities, researchers, and civil society, with safeguards for privacy and personal data. On technology, we must equip justice professionals to respond to rapidly evolving threats and cooperate effectively across borders. Digital tools can improve access to justice and support investigations, but their use requires clear legal safeguards, accountability and meaningful human oversight. Digital transformation must also remain accessible to those who cannot use online services. Mr. President, The European Union will contribute through partnerships, technical assistance, and our Pledge for Justice commitment, including the forthcoming TEMIS and INTERCEPT initiatives. We remain committed to helping partners strengthen criminal justice capacities and cooperation against organized crime and terrorism. Throughout this work, respect for international law, human rights, and the rule of law must remain our foundation. We reiterate our unequivocal opposition to the death penalty in all circumstances. Mr. President, we leave Abu Dhabi with a shared responsibility to ensure that the commitments made here lead to stronger institutions, more effective cooperation, better protection for victims and safer communities. The European Union and its Member States stand ready to work with all partners to fulfil this responsibility. Thank you very much, Mr. President.
